chapter_title: Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space — Core Principles
text: Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space — Complete Textbook Reference (Quantum Mechanics, 56 pages). The Schrodinger equation governs the deterministic unitary time evolution of the complex quantum mechanical wavefunction. Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle states that non-commuting canonical observables cannot simultaneously possess sharp eigenvalues. The Born rule defines the probability density of finding a quantum particle at a given position as the squared modulus of the wavefunction. A Hermitian operator is a linear self-adjoint operator on Hilbert space possessing strictly real observable eigenvalues. Core concepts covered in Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space: schrodinger equation, wavefunction, hermitian operator, eigenstate, commutator, uncertainty principle, harmonic oscillator, pauli matrices.

Version 1.3c Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space [p.4] Version 1.3c Eduardo Mart´ın-Mart´ınez Phase Space Quantum Mechanics Crash-Course on classical phase-space mechanics 1.1 Configuration space and its tangent fibre bundle Consider a physical system with n degrees of freedom, described by a configuration space Q of n dimensions. q) is therefore a map between q and Rn. If there is a compatible collection of such invertible and bicontinuous maps1 mapping an open set2 around all points, q ∈Q to open sets of Rn, the configuration space has a structure of differentiable manifold. For example, a system of two penduli restricted to move on a plane is described with two angular coordinates q1, q2 ∈[0, 2π), therefore the system's configuration space is a torus, Q = T 2 = S1 × S1. The trajectory of the system (how it moves as a function of some evolution parameter, e.g., time) is determined by a parametric curve q(s) in Q, where s ∈R. One can think, for example as the trajectory as a function of time if we identify the parameter s with time. In each point q we can build the tangent vector space TqQ generated by all the possible vectors ˙q which are tangent to every curve that pass through q. These vectors, whose components we denote as ˙qa, represent all the possible 'generalized velocities' that one can have at the point q. The dot symbolizes a derivative with respect to the parameter s, i.e., ˙q = dq/ds. We call the velocity phase space TQ (also called, the tangent fibre bundle to the configuration space Q) the set of all the points q ∈Q together with all their corresponding tangent spaces TqQ. TQ is also a differentiable manifold in its own right. As examples, the configuration space of a pendulum restricted to move on a plane is the circle Q = S1. At each point, the possible values of its velocity are not limited, therefore the tangent space at each point of its trajectory is the real line TqQ = R. The tangent fibre bundle (velocity phase space) is the cylinder TQ = S1 × R. 1The maps are continuous and their inverses are continuous too. (1.54) Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space 2.1 Let's get quantum: Canonical Quantization and its issues We are going to discuss the process of canonical quantization12. This process takes a classical system and a set of its dynamical variables, and returns a quantum system and quantum observables. More specifically, a quantization of a classical system is a linear map - denoted by a hat (ˆ) - from (a subspace of) the space of dynamical observables (functions on phase space) to (a subspace of) the space of self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space. This map is not arbitrary but must satisfy some properties. 11See for instance https://www.oulu.fi/tf/statfys/lecture 2006/notes2.pdf. 12Canonical quantization is not the only process of quantization. However, other methods, such as path integral quantization, share the same drawbacks, albeit they manifest in different ways. Version 1.3c Quantum Mechanics in Phase Space [p.15] Version 1.3c Eduardo Mart´ın-Mart´ınez In the first place it must represent the Poisson bracket structure. To represent that structure when the dynamical variables are linear operators on a Hilbert space, there is a Lie bracket kind of operation that naturally comes to mind: the commutator. Therefore, the quantization map must satisfy [ˆ◦, ˆ◦] = iℏ\ {◦, ◦}. The reason for the imaginary unit to be there is because the Poisson bracket of two dynamical variables is a dynamical variables, and, in contrast, the commutator of two self-adjoint operators is not self-adjoint (but anti-selfadjoint). Ideally, one would like to represent all functions f on phase space (i.e. all physical classical observables) and their Poisson brackets as quantum operators. Second, the representation must be irreducible, so that there exists no proper subspace of the Hilbert space invariant under the action of all the represented observables. If a representation were reducible, it would be the direct sum of irreducible representations that we could study separately. We would then need additional information to select one of them which would introduce additional ambiguities. However, in general, these two conditions are not compatible and it is impossible to map all possible dynamical functions to quantum observables (Groenewold's theorem)13. There are very few cases where the two requisites are compatible so that a quantization of all the classical dynamical variables can be carried out. One such case is the torus, but not in R2. Gaussian Quantum Mechanics 5.1 The covariance matrix and the vector of means We are now going to focus on those states that have a Gaussian Wigner function17. Those states are families of squeezed, coherent thermal states. A Gaussian state's Wigner function can be written as W(ξ) = πnp det(σ) exp -(ξ -ξ0)µ(ξ -ξ0)ν(σ-1)µν (5.1) 17Note that some references may use "Gaussian states" to refer to a larger set, including also all the possible convex combinations of the Gaussian states we define here. Notice that those states' Wigner functions will not be Gaussian in general, although they are positive and therefore they also correspond to classical states (that can be thought of as classical probability distributions over the Gaussian states we define in (5.1)). However, the most common definition for Gaussian state is the one we give in these notes. (5.2) The matrix σ captures the canonical vairable's statistical second moments, i.e., the covariance between each pair of canonical observables, σµν := ˆΞµˆΞν + ˆΞν ˆΞµE ˆρ -2 ˆΞµE ˆΞνE ˆρ . (5.3) Note that there are other conventions for the covariance matrix (e.g., dividing by 2, etc.). This one is one of the most convenient notations. To characterize any Gaussian state it is enough to know its first moments and the covariance matrix, for a total of n(2n + 3) real numbers. There is no need to deal with infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces for these states. The condition of positive definiteness together with the canonical commutation relations implies that σ ≥iΩ-1 where Ω-1 is the matrix inverse of the symplectic matrix (Exercise!). Note that the condition σ ≥iΩ-1 ⇒σ > 0. To prove that the condition σ ≥iΩ-1 implies that the covariance matrix is positive semidefinite, we use that conjugating a positive semidefinite form keeps it positive semidefinite, and we have σ ≥iΩ-1 ⇒σ = σ∗≥(iΩ-1)∗= -iΩ-1 where we have used the fact that σ and Ω-1 are both real valued. Since σ is greater than both iΩ-1 and -iΩ-1, it is greater than their average as well, thus σ ≥0. This implication cannot be reversed. Note that in addition to keeping the covariance matrix positive semidefinite, the condition σ ≥iΩ-1 also enforces the uncertainty principle by preventing the covariances from being arbitrarily small. text: [p.49] Version 1.3c Eduardo Mart´ın-Mart´ınez Entropy and Entanglement of Gaussian states 6.1 Symplectic diagonalization of the covariance matrix Williamson's theorem says that any symmetric positive definite real matrix of even dimensions can be diagonalized by a symplectic transformation: σd = SdσS⊺ (6.1) where the matrix σd is diagonal and of the form σd = i=1 νi ... (6.2) Notice that a symplectic transformation defines a change of canonical coordinates, and therefore Williamson's theorem is saying that there always exist a set of canonical coordinates ˜ξµ such that the symplectic matrix is the direct sum of harmonic oscillators in thermal states, one per mode in the system! This is equivalent to matrix σ, and we call symplectic eigenvalues to every element of the symplectic spectrum. It is important to note that the symplectic eigenvalues are not the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix. We can find a relationship between the eigenvalues of σ and its symplectic eigenvalues. To do this let us first define a matrix M := σΩ-1. Let us evaluate how M transforms under a symplectic transformation of the covariance matrix: M ′ = SσS⊺Ω-1 = SσS⊺(S⊺)-1Ω-1S-1 = SσΩ-1S-1 = SMS-1. (6.3) Here we have used that SΩS⊺= Ω⇒(S⊺)-1Ω-1S-1 = Ω-1. So we see that the symplectic transformation of the covariance matrix induces a similarity transformation on M that leaves the eigenvalues of M invariant. If we particularize now to the symplectic transformation that symplectically diagonalizes σ to the form (6.2), then the explicit form of M ′ = σdΩ-1 is M ′ = i=1  0 -νi (6.4) and therefore the eigenvalues of M are {±iνi}. We conclude that the symplectic eigenvalues of S are the modulus of the eigenvalues of σΩ-1. This shows as well that the symplectic eigenvalues are invariant under any symplectic transformation. The symplectic eigenvalues, as we will see, contain all the information about any entanglement present in a Gaussian state. Finding the symplectic eigenvalues of a covariance matrix is a much easier endeavour than finding the eigenvalues of the corresponding density matrix. Given a real symmetric positive definite matrix F of even dimension 2n, we want to find the symplectic transformation Σ that satisfies ΣF Σ⊺= i=1 νi ≡F, (6.5) of F Ω-1, which we know how to calculate with basic linear algebra techniques. The algorithm to perform the symplectic diagonalization goes as follows: we look for a symplectic transformation with the form Σ = F1/2OF -1/2, (6.6) where O is an orthogonal matrix. Notice that F1/2 can be calculated straightforwardly, since F is diagonal. To calculate F -1/2, we need to first diagonalize it (by similarity, in the usual sense), then perform the inverse and the square root, and then reverse the diagonalization. With a Σ of the form (6.6), we get that ΣF Σ⊺= F1/2OF -1/2F F -1/2O⊺F1/2 = F1/2OO⊺F1/2 = F, (6.7) where we used that F and F are symmetric, and the orthogonality of O. Demarie in arXiv:1209.2748. Let us consider a system of N continuous variable degrees of freedom. The state of the system is the arbitrary Gaussian state with density operator ˆρ and associated covariance matrix σ. One can always find a (symplectic) transformation S that symplectically diagonalizes σ so that σ′ = SσS⊺is its Williamson form. Such a symplectic transformation maps the quadrature operators to their primed versions ˆΞ′ = S ˆΞ. This symplectic transformation is associated to an unitary transformation in the Hilbert space ˆU such that ˆρ′ = ˆU ˆρ ˆU† corresponds to the state of coveraince matrix σ′. Thus, we can write ˆρ′ as ˆρ′ = ˆρ′ 1 ⊗ˆρ′ (6.16) where ˆρ′ i is the density operator of a single quantum harmonic oscillator in a thermal state. We know this because, as we saw in Sec. 5, a diagonal covariance matrix can always be read as a thermal state of a set of uncoupled harmonic oscillators. Note that the primed oscillators are now uncoupled, although each oscillator is non-local, as each mode is a linear combination of possibly many of the original modes. Recall that the thermal equilibrium state of a harmonic oscillator at temperature T is represented by the Gibbs state we saw in previous sections.
